title: Connecting Goals to Criticism Shows Others Youre Trying to Help and Not Hurt Them
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that people evaluate feedback almost entirely through the lens of the giver's perceived intent, meaning even accurate criticism will be resisted if the recipient doubts it's meant to help. It explains that because feedback commonly carries negative information, receivers default to suspicion, assuming the giver may be trying to hurt rather than help unless proven otherwise. The recommended technique is to state the specific goal or desired outcome before delivering the feedback itself, since a clear goal makes benevolent intent far more transparent than simply declaring good intentions out loud. The piece closes by tying this practice directly to the ultimate purpose of feedback, changing behavior, calling anything else "just catharsis, or worse."
points: Feedback is judged almost entirely through the perceived intent of the giver, not just the accuracy of the content.
Because feedback often carries negative information, receivers default to suspecting harmful intent unless clearly shown otherwise.
Stating the specific goal or desired outcome before delivering feedback makes benevolent intent transparent more effectively than simply declaring good intentions.
The article ties the technique directly back to feedback's real purpose: changing behavior, not venting.
quotes: People don’t separate the content of feedback from the person giving it.
For the feedback to land successfully, those on the receiving end must believe the giver is trying to make them better and improve their performance.
Because many leaders, parents, and coaches use feedback as a weapon to torment or wound others, people are on guard against negative intentions.
The best leaders do something remarkably simple to clarify their positive intentions: They tie the feedback to specific goals and outcomes before offering it.
And that’s always your goal with feedback—to change behavior or improve performance. Anything else is just catharsis — or worse.
